title: NURS 1017 Unit 3 Case Study 7

question.stem: The nurse reviews the client's history and assessment. Which findings are risk factors for a congenital anomaly in this pregnancy? Select all that apply.

options.text: No MMR vaccine, with fever, rash and swollen nodes behind the ears at 5 weeks of gestation
No folic acid before conception
Started a prenatal vitamin with iron at 10 weeks
Valproic acid 500 mg twice daily throughout early pregnancy
Isotretinoin 40 mg daily until 6 weeks of gestation
BP 114/70 mm Hg and BMI 23.2 kg/m²
Partner's sister's son was born with spina bifida
Age 28 years, first pregnancy

question.explanation:
Risk factors: isotretinoin (a vitamin A derivative) is one of the most potent known teratogens (Option 5). Rubella infection in early pregnancy can cross the placenta and cause congenital rubella syndrome; the rash, fever and posterior auricular nodes during an outbreak in a non-immune client suggest primary infection (Option 1). Valproic acid raises the risk of neural tube defects and other malformations and impairs brain development (Option 4). Folic acid taken before conception lowers the risk of neural tube defects; she had none, while taking a folate antagonist (Option 2). Neural tube defects are multifactorial: a relative with spina bifida (here, a cousin of the baby) adds some genetic susceptibility (Option 7).

Timing: gestational age is counted from the last menstrual period, about 2 weeks before conception. The embryonic period, when organs form, runs from about 3 to 8 weeks after conception, or about 5 to 10 weeks of gestation. Her rubella infection, isotretinoin and valproic acid all overlapped it.

Not risk factors: age 28 does not raise the risk of chromosomal conditions the way maternal age over 35 does (Option 8). BP and BMI are normal (Option 6). Starting a prenatal vitamin is healthy, though too late to prevent a neural tube defect (Option 3).

leftContent.intro: The nurse in a maternal-fetal medicine clinic is completing a first prenatal visit for Elena, a 28-year-old client (G1P0) at 10 weeks and 2 days of gestation.

question.stem: The nurse prepares teaching about the possible effects of each exposure. For each fetal or newborn finding, click to specify whether it is most closely associated with isotretinoin, rubella virus, or valproic acid.

rows.text: Small or absent external ears and a small jaw
Patent ductus arteriosus and purple “blueberry muffin” skin lesions
Conotruncal heart defect with a small thymus
Lower IQ and higher rates of autism spectrum disorder in childhood

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1100 and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Isotretinoin: a retinoid that disrupts neural crest cells, which form much of the face, ears, thymus and the heart's outflow tract. Typical findings are small or absent ears (microtia, anotia), a small jaw, conotruncal heart defects (such as tetralogy of Fallot), thymic hypoplasia and brain malformations.

Rubella virus: a TORCH infection. Positive IgM with low-avidity IgG confirms a recent primary infection. Infection in the first trimester can cause congenital rubella syndrome: cataracts, sensorineural hearing loss and heart defects (especially patent ductus arteriosus), with growth restriction, microcephaly and purpuric skin lesions in the newborn.

Valproic acid: antagonizes folate and disrupts neural tube closure, raising the risk of spina bifida (myelomeningocele) about tenfold; it also impairs brain development throughout pregnancy, lowering IQ and increasing autism spectrum disorder. Her level is therapeutic and her folate is low.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: Isotretinoin, rubella virus and valproic acid are each a [[drop0]]: an outside agent that disrupts development without changing the genes the child will pass on. Because Elena's exposures occurred during [[drop1]], the main risk is a structural malformation. The nurse's priority regarding valproic acid is [[drop2]].

options.text: mutagen
allele
mutation
teratogen
the fetal period (from 9 weeks after conception)
the third trimester
the pre-implantation period (first 2 weeks after conception)
the embryonic period (3 to 8 weeks after conception)
reassuring her that the risk ended once the neural tube closed
advising her not to stop it on her own and arranging a prompt neurology review
advising her to skip doses on days she feels well to lower fetal exposure
advising her to stop it tonight because it is a known teratogen

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1145.
question.explanation:
Teratogen: an outside agent (medicine, infection, alcohol, radiation) that causes a congenital anomaly by disrupting development. The child's genes are unchanged, so the anomaly is not passed on to the child's own children. A mutagen changes DNA, and a mutation is a change in DNA.

Embryonic period: about 3 to 8 weeks after conception (5 to 10 weeks of gestation), when the organs form, so exposures cause major structural malformations. Exposures in the first 2 weeks tend to have an all-or-none effect (pregnancy loss or no harm); in the fetal period they mainly affect growth and function, including brain development.

Valproic acid: stopping an antiseizure medicine abruptly can cause seizures or status epilepticus, with maternal and fetal hypoxia, injury or pregnancy loss. Skipping doses has the same danger. The neural tube closes about 28 days after conception, but valproic acid still affects the developing brain, so its use is reviewed promptly by neurology. Any change is directed and supervised by the neurologist.

question.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include in Elena's plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give the MMR vaccine today to protect the fetus from further rubella effects
Teach Elena to take folic acid 4 mg daily and keep her MSAFP, anatomy ultrasound and fetal echocardiogram appointments
Reinforce that Elena follows the neurologist's medication change plan rather than stopping on her own
Confirm that Elena has stopped isotretinoin and returns any remaining capsules to the pharmacy
Teach Elena to avoid alcohol, tobacco, and unnecessary X-rays or CT scans for the rest of the pregnancy
Offer non-directive emotional support and confirm the genetic counselling appointment
Tell Elena to stop all seizure medicines until after the baby is born

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1330 and the Care Plan.
question.explanation:
Include: confirming that isotretinoin has stopped prevents further exposure (Option 4). Following the neurologist's supervised plan protects mother and fetus from seizures (Option 3). Folic acid 4 mg daily is recommended in pregnancy for clients taking antiseizure medicines; it can no longer prevent a neural tube defect that would already have formed, so MSAFP and the anatomy ultrasound check for one, and the fetal echocardiogram checks the heart (Option 2). Non-directive counselling supports Elena while respecting her own decisions (Option 6). Avoiding alcohol (fetal alcohol spectrum disorder), tobacco (growth restriction) and unnecessary radiation prevents further harm (Option 5).

Do not include: MMR is a live vaccine and is not given in pregnancy; it cannot treat an infection that has already occurred. A non-immune client receives it after delivery (Option 1). Stopping antiseizure medicine risks life-threatening seizures (Option 7).

leftContent.intro: The nurse works with maternal-fetal medicine, neurology and genetic counselling on Elena's plan of care.

question.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether the action is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated.

rows.text: Give the MMR vaccine today so Elena becomes immune to rubella
Reinforce taking levetiracetam as prescribed and reporting any seizure activity
Request a maternal karyotype to check whether isotretinoin changed Elena's chromosomes
Request an abdominal CT scan to give Elena a clearer picture of the baby
Confirm the dates of the MSAFP, detailed anatomy ultrasound and fetal echocardiogram
Document a reminder to give the MMR vaccine after delivery

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1015 (14 weeks) and the Vital Signs.
question.explanation:
MMR today (Contraindicated): live vaccines (MMR, varicella) are not given in pregnancy because of the theoretical risk to the fetus.

Seizure control (Indicated): stable seizure control during and after the medication change prevents maternal and fetal hypoxia and injury.

Maternal karyotype (Non-Essential): isotretinoin is a teratogen: it disrupts the embryo's development and does not change the mother's chromosomes. A karyotype would add nothing.

CT for a clearer picture (Contraindicated): CT exposes the fetus to ionizing radiation, a physical teratogen, without any benefit here. Fetal anatomy is assessed with ultrasound (and MRI without gadolinium if needed). A single diagnostic CT is below the dose linked to malformations, so it is not withheld when truly needed, but it is never done for a picture of the baby.

Screening dates (Indicated): MSAFP screens for open neural tube defects; the detailed anatomy ultrasound and fetal echocardiogram look for structural and heart defects.

MMR after delivery (Indicated): it is safe during breastfeeding and protects future pregnancies from congenital rubella.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: Elena shows understanding of her partner's family history when she describes spina bifida as [[drop0]]. To lower the risk of a congenital anomaly in a future pregnancy, Elena states she will [[drop1]]. She correctly explains that an anomaly caused by a teratogen [[drop2]].

options.text: autosomal recessive: both parents must be carriers
X-linked recessive: passed from carrier mothers to sons
chromosomal: caused by an extra chromosome
multifactorial: several genes interacting with factors such as folate
rely on an early ultrasound in her next pregnancy to prevent birth defects
stop her seizure medicine as soon as she has a positive pregnancy test
take folic acid and review her seizure medicine with neurology before trying to conceive
get the MMR vaccine early in her next pregnancy, once it is confirmed
will happen again in each of her future pregnancies
changes the child's karyotype
is passed on to half of the child's children
is not passed on to the child's own children

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1400 (20 weeks) and the Diagnostic Results.
question.explanation:
Multifactorial: neural tube defects, cleft lip and palate and many heart defects come from several genes plus environmental factors (low folate, valproic acid, maternal diabetes). They do not follow Mendelian ratios; the risk rises modestly with each affected relative. Normal MSAFP and an intact spine on ultrasound make a neural tube defect very unlikely in this pregnancy.

Before the next pregnancy: organs form 3 to 8 weeks after conception, often before a pregnancy is known, so prevention starts before conception: folic acid, a neurology review of antiseizure medicines, confirmed rubella immunity (MMR at least 4 weeks before conceiving, never during pregnancy), two forms of contraception during any isotretinoin treatment, and no alcohol. Stopping medicine abruptly is dangerous, and ultrasound detects anomalies but cannot prevent them.

Not inherited: a teratogen changes development, not the child's genes, so the anomaly is not passed to the next generation. It recurs in a later pregnancy only if the exposure recurs. The ventricular septal defect and mild growth lag may relate to rubella or isotretinoin; the newborn will be assessed at birth.
